gaps.sentence: He passed all his exams first time, ___ surprised everyone.
gaps.hint: refers to the whole previous clause
gaps.explanation: 'Which' can refer to a whole idea ('he passed first time'); this non-defining use never takes 'that'.

gaps.sentence: Our new neighbours, ___ have three children, moved in last week.
gaps.hint: people as subject; clause between commas
gaps.explanation: 'Who' is used for people in non-defining clauses; 'which' is for things.

gaps.sentence: The winner, ___ was only seventeen, broke the championship record.
gaps.hint: person as subject after a comma
gaps.explanation: The clause adds extra information about a person, so 'who' is required and 'that' is impossible.

gaps.sentence: She told me ___ had happened, but I didn't believe her.
gaps.explanation: 'What had happened' means 'the things that had happened'; 'that' cannot stand alone as the subject here.

gaps.sentence: The lawyers, against ___ the case was brought, denied everything.
gaps.hint: the case was brought against them
gaps.explanation: 'Against whom' is the formal relative pattern; 'who' and 'that' cannot follow prepositions.

gaps.sentence: He repaired the car ___ engine had failed.
gaps.hint: the engine belongs to the car
gaps.explanation: 'Whose engine' means 'the car's engine', showing possession even with objects.

gaps.sentence: The author, about ___ there has been much debate, will speak at the festival.
gaps.hint: debate about the author — person after preposition
gaps.explanation: 'About whom' is required after the preposition 'about' when referring to a person.

gaps.sentence: The letter ___ arrived this morning is from my aunt.
gaps.explanation: 'Which' refers to the letter, a thing, as the subject of 'arrived'.
